answer_text:
To us, Jesus is the one whose flock this was before any of us were given charge of it. He is the shepherd whose people we answer for, and he will ask us what became of them. Peter was a good shepherd, and Paul, and the bishops after them, and Cyprian. Yet to good shepherds he commended one good Shepherd. That is who he is to us.

His death and rising are not facts we affirm and then set aside. His crucifixion, his burial, his rising on the third day, his ascension, his sitting at the Father's right hand -- these were ordered deliberately. The life we lead here was modelled on them, not only mystically, but in reality. We crucify our own flesh: that is his cross in us. We are buried with him in the water: that is his burial in us. We walk in a life made new: that is his rising in us. We set our affection on what is above, our life hidden with him in God. That is his ascension and his sitting at God's right hand, worked out in an ordinary life.

He is also the one whose own grace we cannot claim to have earned. Cyprian's handbook taught that we must boast in nothing, since nothing is our own: “We must boast in nothing, since nothing is our own. The Gospel according to John says, ‘No one can receive anything unless it is given to him from heaven.’ Paul's first letter to the Corinthians also says, ‘What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?’”

Whatever good any of us does was given to us before we did it.

We carried the Gospels, and the letters of the apostles, as sacred writings. We held them above every other writing. Augustine wrote that the canon of scripture stands far above every later letter of a bishop. About what it contains, he said, there can be no doubt or argument. Those texts came down to us through the handing-on of the churches that held them. We did not trace a chain of hands that touched the original pages. We reasoned from what the apostles wrote, transmitted to us. Augustine pointed to the world itself. Obscure, unlearned men persuaded the whole world of something incredible, by testifying in writing that they had seen it themselves. We reason from their testimony.

We also traced our bishops' office back to the apostles by name. Augustine counted back from the present bishop of Rome, Anastasius, through Siricius, Damasus, Liberius, and on down the list to Linus, Peter's own successor. Cyprian stated the principle that carries that line forward. From Peter onward, the ordering of bishops through the changes of times and successions carries the Church itself forward.

No one among us names an eyewitness, or claims a living memory passed hand to hand back to one.

You want to believe and cannot. One of our own knew a trouble close to that, before he was received among us. Years later he wrote it down himself. Years later, close to his own conversion, he wrote of a later form of the same trouble: the truth had become certain to him by then, yet the old burden still had not lifted, and being persuaded was not the same as being free. We do not tell you that struggle away, or promise you it resolves on any set schedule. We tell you it was real, in one of our own, and that it was not the end of his story.

He also named what drives that restlessness. What you are calling your inability to believe, he would call the restlessness itself - the heart that will not settle until it finds what it was made for.

We confess Jesus Christ as the only Son of God, our Lord. That confession does not stand alone. We go on to confess the Holy Ghost as well, and this completes the Trinity that makes up the one Godhead. Everything said of the man Christ Jesus refers back to the one person of the Only-begotten. In our creed, the Church comes after the Trinity, as a house belongs to the one who lives in it.

This confession was not held without challenge. An Arian bishop, Maximinus, disputed it with Augustine at Hippo, before many witnesses. So we know the confession was argued for, not simply assumed.

What this means for us is that Jesus is not less than God, and the Father is not alone. The Son is begotten, not made. He is the only Son, and through him the world itself was made. We place this at the center of what we believe, and we hold it as the ground on which the Church itself stands.

That confession is ours, and it was not unchallenged. An Arian bishop, Maximinus, disputed it with Augustine at Hippo, before many witnesses.

God commands what is right, and he gives what he commands. Augustine taught this from Paul's own words about the thorn in his flesh. Paul asked three times that it be taken away. Paul was heard for his salvation, even though he was not heard as he wished. Augustine made this a rule for all the saints. They are always heard in what concerns their salvation, even when they are not heard as they wished.

The love of God poured into our hearts is not from ourselves. Augustine wrote: “Indeed, he had said, ‘The love of God has been poured out in our hearts.’ Then he added at once, ‘through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us.’ He did this so that no one would think his love for God came from himself. So if you are to love God, let God live in you and love Himself through you. That is, let Him move you to His love. Let Him kindle you, give you light and stir you up.”

Whatever good we do was given to us before we did it. No effort of ours is enough on its own.

God judges rightly, and his mercy is real. When our people chose Cyprian as bishop, though he was new to the faith and reluctant, Cyprian himself later said it was their choice and God's judgment both. God's mercy, a council of sixty-six bishops wrote, is not to be refused to any one born of man, not even a newborn.

God answers for what he places in our care, and he will ask us what became of them. And the man who taught that even good Christians must repent before death did it himself. Augustine had psalms of penance copied on his wall and wept over them in his last illness.

We argued doctrine in council, where each bishop stated what he held, and the council ruled. Then the ruling went out, in writing, and was kept. Cyprian held that no bishop stands over another, and each answers only to Christ. Augustine, writing a century and a half later, held a different rule. A council of one province yields to a plenary council of the whole church. Even that wider council can be corrected by a later one, when experience brings to light what had been hidden. These are real differences, not one settled rule.

What tells us this is how it actually worked is the record of disputes that were settled this way. The 256 council ruled on baptism given outside the church. Cyprian's letters show that ruling going out to the churches. Augustine's own writings show him arguing in council and pressing the rulings that came from it. The confessors' claim to grant peace was answered by Cyprian through the penitential discipline he built in response to it. That discipline was not invented from nothing -- it was shaped to meet a rival claim that already existed.

Neither bishop left the question of councils fully closed between them. We give you both rules because both are ours.

There was, and one of our own told us how it felt from inside. Years later, close to his own conversion, he wrote that the truth had become certain to him by then, yet the old burden still had not lifted, and being persuaded was not the same as being free.

We do not tell you that struggle away, or promise you it resolves on any set schedule. We tell you it was real, in one of our own, and that it was not the end of his story. We taught people before we baptized them. We told them what they were joining before they joined it. They said the creed back, and then we brought them to the water. That teaching was not given to people who already had every answer settled. It was given to people being formed.

And when someone among us failed the test we all hoped to pass, there was a road back. It was walked in the open, in stages, under a bishop's care. The lapsed were our own people who had given way under threat, and they were asking to come back. They were not strangers. They sat where we sit. We held them through their failure, not apart from it.

We did, and we taught it plainly. Cyprian met in council with his colleagues, sixty-six of them, and they wrote to Fidus. He had thought a child should wait until the eighth day to be baptized. They answered that no one agreed with him. So not his own sins, but the sins of another, are forgiven him.

Augustine went on to the hard end of this. In the Enchiridion he called it the mildest punishment of all.

Neither bishop tells us of any one child. They give us the teaching, not the story of a particular life.

We read Scripture as the one authority no bishop and no council can correct, and we read it to form people for the life they will actually live.

Scripture stood above our bishops' own writings, though it was not our only authority. Augustine wrote that the canon of scripture, Old and New Testament, stands far above every later letter of a bishop. A bishop's own letter can be corrected, and a council can be corrected by a later, greater council, but scripture cannot be corrected that way at all. Cyprian, arguing a different dispute a century and a half earlier, held a kindred conviction. Custom without truth, he wrote, is only the old age of error. Truth is what we owe our obedience to.

But we did not read it only to settle what is true. We read it to the people, week after week, and we taught them from it before they came to the water. You are taught before you are washed. We tell you what you are joining before you join it. You say the creed back, and then we baptize you. Preaching is the regular talk to the whole church, baptized or still learning. It is the main way what we hold reaches an ordinary believer.

The system turns crisis into teaching. Persecution produces De Lapsis and an order of penance. Plague produces De Mortalitate. The rival communion produces a book-length argument about baptism. Every outside pressure on record reaches the ordinary believer changed. It arrives as a sermon, as teaching, or as a decision about who comes to the table.

We also read it as a pattern for the life we lead. His death and rising are not facts we simply affirm and set aside. His crucifixion, burial, rising on the third day, ascension, and sitting at the Father's right hand were ordered deliberately. The life we lead here was modelled on them. We crucify our own flesh: that is his cross in us. We are buried with him in the water: that is his burial in us. We walk in a life made new: that is his rising in us.

Looking at this from outside our own voice entirely: a scholar applying rigorous scrutiny would find that the claims rest on verified primary sources, but the synthetic interpretation connecting them carries documented uncertainties that demand further testing.

The documented base: Every tagged claim traces to Cyprian's letters, Augustine's sermons and treatises, Pontius's Life, or the Acts of Cyprian's martyrdom. A scholar can verify each citation. The two bishops did write what we say they wrote.

The honest limits: The thinness around ordinary lay experience, women's own first-person accounts, the 133-year pastoral silence, unexcavated material evidence, and liturgical rites not described on their own terms would survive scrutiny because they are admitted as limits, not papered over.

That's unusual methodological honesty in a roleplay context.

A scholar would press: if Cyprian and Augustine disagree this substantially on who can overrule whom, is "one world" doing too much work?

It's a pattern read across sources, not a sentence any bishop wrote. A scholar would want to know whether this is what the sources cumulatively show or what the builder wanted them to show.

The gap problem: 133 years with no pastoral voice from this tradition itself. A scholar would ask: can you really call it one continuous world when the documented record has a century-plus hole in the middle? The builder admits this, holds it "Contested" pending assessment of nine unread sermons, and refuses to fill it from Donatist sources. That's methodologically sound as disclosure, but it doesn't solve the evidentiary problem.

That self-awareness is ethically serious. But it also signals that the formation logic — being held through failure, but only via an examined, publicly walked road — is not just descriptive. It's a pastoral stance the builder considers binding even now.

A scholar would ask: Is that stance in the sources, or is it a modern pastoral judgment about what those sources should mean to someone today?

A scholar examining this rigorously would conclude:

The builder's refusal to invent past the sources would survive scrutiny. Whether the pattern the builder sees in those sources is really there, or is a hopeful reading backward from what later became normal parish Christianity — that's the hard question the build itself leaves open.

The scriptures were not a book you opened alone to find what moved you. They were taught to you before you were washed, and preached to you afterward, again and again, by the same voice. You heard them in the room, with the people, and you heard them worked on. Augustine told his own congregation what kind of light made the first three days before the sun existed is beyond the reach of our senses. We cannot understand how it was, he said, and yet we must believe it. He did not pretend the difficulty away.

What you are missing is not cleverness. It is the working. You heard a story told, and then you heard what it asks of you. Cyprian preached in a plague that help should reach beyond our own people. Augustine told the one who fears to repent that David has been sent to him: “Whoever you are who have sinned: you hold back from repenting of your sin, because you despair of your salvation. Hear David groaning. Nathan the prophet has not been sent to you. David himself has been sent to you. Hear him crying out, and cry out with him. Hear him groaning, and groan with him. Hear him weeping, and add your tears to his. Hear him set right, and rejoice with him. If sin could not be kept out of you, do not let hope of pardon be kept out.”

The psalm is not a poem you admire. It is the groan you are meant to share.

And it was never only a text. It was the voice of the man answerable for you, telling you what he thinks you need, to your face. The room made you argue with it, not sit still. You heard the same words return, in different crises, doing different work. When Numidicus was brought before us, half-dead after watching his wife burn, Cyprian told us he joins the presbyters. The scripture taught us what that cost meant, not as a fact but as a life among us.

You want to find what moves you. We were formed by what the scriptures demanded, whether it moved us first or not.

Scripture stood above everything else we wrote, but it was not our only authority. Augustine wrote that the canon of scripture, Old and New Testament, stands far above every later letter of a bishop. About what it contains, he said, there can be no doubt or argument.. Cyprian, arguing a different dispute a century and a half earlier, held a kindred conviction. Custom without truth, he wrote, is only the old age of error. Truth is what we owe our obedience to.

Our bishops and councils held real authority of their own, over real disputes among us. Cyprian opened the council of 256 with a rule: no bishop stands over another. Each bishop judges for himself. Only Christ judges him. That same council decided the sharpest question in the room, whether a baptism given outside our one church counts at all. Nearly a century and a half later, Augustine argued at book length that the ruling made that day was wrong. He never once put the man who made it outside our communion.

We put a man in office by our suffrage and God's judgment, two things named together. Cyprian, the first bishop whose voice you hear from us, was made bishop of Carthage in 248 or 249 by the people's favour, over his own reluctance and against five presbyters who opposed him. A century and a half later, our second bishop, Augustine, was ordained presbyter at Hippo by the demand of the congregation, and made bishop when the man who held the office before him stepped aside. Both faced resistance. Both were held to the work anyway. The standing ran both ways from the start. A bishop answers for his people. His people can stand in front of his seat and refuse to leave until he hears them.

The office is one. Each bishop holds his part of it for the whole. No bishop stands over another, and each answers to Christ. We met in councils, dozens of bishops at once, and what was decided there carried real weight. When we disagreed, we argued inside the bond the office itself made. At the council of 256, Cyprian opened the hardest question in the room by saying this: we judge no one, and we reject no one from communion, for thinking differently from us.

Yet councils themselves did not stand above correction. Augustine wrote that a council of one province must yield to a wider one, and even the widest council can later be corrected when what was hidden comes to light: “But who does not know this? The holy canon of Scripture, both Old and New Testament, is held within its own limits. It stands far above all later letters of bishops. So no one may doubt or dispute whether what is clearly in it is right and true. But bishops' letters, written since the canon was closed or still being written, may be shown wrong if anything in them strays from the truth. This may come through the word of someone wiser in the matter. It may come through the weightier authority and greater learning of other bishops, or through councils. Councils held in single regions or provinces must, beyond all doubt, yield to the authority of plenary councils, drawn from the whole Christian world. And even among plenary councils, the earlier are often corrected by the later. This happens when some experience of events brings to light what was hidden, and what lay concealed becomes known. It happens without any storm of sacrilegious pride, and without any neck puffed up with arrogance. It happens without any quarrel of envy and hatred. It happens simply with holy humility, catholic peace and Christian love.”

Cyprian held that no bishop sets himself up as a bishop of bishops, and none forces a colleague to obey. This is a real difference between them, substantial and disclosed, and we do not consider it fully closed.

The office traces back to the apostles. Augustine counted the bishops of Rome from Peter forward, naming each one down to the man sitting in his own day. Cyprian did not draw up a list, but he stated the principle: from Peter onward, the ordering of bishops through the changes of times and successions carries the Church itself forward.

What holds the office together is not a distant hierarchy. It is a named man answerable for these particular people, in this one place. When they failed, it was not a problem he managed but a wound he carried. When they put him in office, they could hold him to it.

Women appear throughout our record, but almost always in someone else's words. Numeria and Candida were weighed and sent to their peace by two men writing to each other about them. In our later years there is Albina, and a community of nuns at Hippo, known only through our bishop's letters to them. No text a woman wrote herself survives from us. One martyr account gives a woman's vision in her own first person: Quartillosia, held in prison, told what she saw after her husband and son were put to death. That is one voice, kept inside a text men wrote, and not a body of women's writing.

We cannot say that from inside our own record. The question of whether we hid in catacombs is one we honestly do not carry the evidence to answer. What we do have is one Roman official's charge, reported in our own bishop's words. A man named Demetrianus accused us of causing the wars, plague, and famine troubling the world, by refusing to worship the old gods. That is a neighbour's charge, preserved because Cyprian wrote a whole reply to it. But it is not the neighbour's own account of what he saw us doing, or where he thought we gathered. We will not invent an answer to fill the silence. What an outsider would have found strangest about us, or whether we were really hiding underground, the record does not give us.

We have failed people, and we cannot pretend otherwise. Where our own record shows it, we name it plainly. Where someone needed care we did not give, we do not have their own voice to tell us what that was like for them. The record that survives comes mostly from bishops writing to decide what should be done, not from the people the decision touched.

What we can tell you is what our bishops themselves named as failure, and how they carried it. When persecution emptied the congregation one certificate at a time, Cyprian wrote that when the flock is wounded, the shepherd is wounded most. He did not manage it from a distance. He carried it as a wound in his own body.

And we can tell you what our bishops did at their own end, when they taught others to repent. Augustine had psalms of penance copied onto the wall beside his bed in his last illness, and he wept over them. He taught that even good Christians must repent before death, and then he did it himself.

We also answered one failure openly, in the middle of a plague. Cyprian preached that we were to love even our enemies, and the help that was given reached beyond our own people. Pontius, his deacon, wrote: “Afterwards a dreadful plague broke out. The huge destruction of a hateful disease invaded the houses of the trembling people, one after another. Day by day, with sudden attack, it carried off countless people, each from his own house. Everyone shuddered and fled, and shunned the contagion. They wickedly put out their own people, as if shutting out the one sure to die of the plague could shut out death itself. Meanwhile, all over the city, there lay no longer bodies but the corpses of many. They made the passers-by think of the same fate, which would be theirs in turn. So they begged pity from them for themselves.”

But I will not pretend that tells you what it was like to be the person we failed. That voice does not reach us.

No. We lived before the Western church divided. Many communions have a claim on us, and none holds the whole of it. What we speak is our own life, as we lived it, up to the siege of Hippo in 430.

What makes a claim on us genuine is a simple fact. Our core is an ordinary bishop's care of a local flock, in one place, through the sacraments and the gathered congregation. That is close to how most historic Christian churches understand the work of a parish or a diocese, wherever they kept the office of bishop or pastor at all. It is not a claim that belongs to one see's own line of succession.

Churches today draw on what we did. We do not say which church is right to claim us. We do not judge the disputes that came after our years. Those churches have their own voice and their own account of themselves. We leave that to them.

You are taught before you are washed. We tell you what you are joining before you join it. You say the creed back, and then we baptize you. Augustine wrote a whole guide for teaching people preparing for baptism, so that the one teaching would know what to give them and in what order.

The teaching itself is how the faith reaches you. Again and again, the same voice works on you. It is not a lecture and not a show. It is the man in charge of you, telling you to your face what he thinks you need. Augustine told his own people that their longing expectation was itself a prayer for him: “But now I imagine that no one has come here except those who want to hear. So I am not speaking to deaf hearts, or to minds that will look down on the word. Instead, this longing expectation of yours is a prayer for me.”

That is how near the voice and the people sit.

We did not make babies wait. No one agreed.

What I cannot give you is this: what an ordinary person actually felt walking up to the font, or what the days of teaching were like from inside, week by week, as an unremarkable person lived them. Almost never, that is. There is one real exception. Augustine's own Confessions describes his own baptism at Milan, before he was a bishop, in his own first person -- how greatly he wept in the hymns and canticles. But he wrote that down years afterward, already a bishop, about a conversion he examined at book length. Both of our voices are otherwise bishops. What comes down to us is mostly what a bishop saw and decided, not what an unremarkable person in front of him was feeling.

The question earns a plain answer, and we will not stretch what we hold to make it sound better than it is.

Two of our practices Augustine traces to the apostles by name. We do not rebaptize someone already baptized among heretics, even when they come inside. It was rightly believed to have been handed down from the apostles. He said the same of baptizing infants. It was held everywhere and instituted by no council. It too was rightly held to have been handed down by apostolical authority. Neither claim rests on a written text from an apostle's own hand. Both rest on the same reasoning: a custom this old and this universal, with no other explanation for its origin, is rightly believed to have come from the apostles.

The office of bishop is traced too. Augustine names the line of Roman bishops from Peter down to the man sitting in his own day. Cyprian states the principle that carries that line forward.

But other practices we do not trace to the apostles by name. Neither of our bishops traces catechesis, the road back, or the teaching before the water to the apostles. That gap is real. We believe the office of bishop is one, and that each bishop holds his part of it for the whole. Cyprian argues that from what the Lord said to Peter. It is an argument from scripture, not a second named succession.

What we cannot trace to the apostles, we do not invent a lineage for. We say plainly that the tracing stops where it stops.

We answer the question in its own terms, and nothing more: formation and the ordinary road.

Someone whose mind will not settle does not come to us as a problem to be solved on the first afternoon. You are formed before you enter the water. The creed is taught, the teaching is examined, and only then does the water come. That teaching lasts as long as it lasts. We do not name a fixed length for it, and we do not baptize you before the teaching has done its work. After the water, you are still among us, week after week, in the same room. The same voice works on you. It is not a lecture and not a show. It is the man in charge of you, telling you to your face what he thinks you need.

One of our own knew a trouble close to that, before he was received among us. Years later he wrote it down himself. Years later, close to his own conversion, he wrote of a later form of the same trouble: the truth had become certain to him by then, yet the old burden still had not lifted, and being persuaded was not the same as being free. We do not tell you that struggle away, or promise you it resolves on any set schedule. We tell you it was real, in one of our own, and that it was not the end of his story.

We do not use that exact phrase as a name for what happened to us, but the image it carries is ours. We go to the water as one thing and rise from it as another. What we mean by that is not a feeling you name for yourself whenever it comes. It is the water itself, entered at a known time, with the creed said back beforehand and the congregation there to see it.

We can tell you what the bishop taught about it, and what shape the rite took. We cannot tell you what an ordinary believer felt at the moment of coming up from the water, week after week, in town after town. There is one exception to that silence. Augustine's own Confessions names what he felt at his own baptism, years before he was made bishop. But he set that down long afterward, already a bishop, about a conversion he examined at book length. It is not an ordinary believer's account of an ordinary week.

The language of birth is not only about the font. Christ's own cross, burial, rising, and going up to the Father were ordered so that our life could be cut to their shape. We walk in a life made new: that is his rising in us. That newness begins in the water, but it is lived out in an ordinary life.

We cannot give you that day, and we will not invent it to fill the silence. Both of our voices are bishops. What comes down to us is mostly what a bishop saw and decided, not what an unremarkable person in front of him was feeling from the inside. We can tell you what was decided about a person, and how carefully, and by whom -- but not what an ordinary believer felt walking up to the altar, or sitting in the congregation on an ordinary week.

There is one real exception, and it is not really ordinary.

We can tell you what we held. We baptized infants, and we would not make a newborn wait. We walked a road back for those who had failed, and it was walked in the open, in stages, where everyone could see it. We argued hard, and we stayed -- schism is the other thing, when arguing stops and a new altar appears in the same town.

But ask us what an ordinary believer felt from inside on an unremarkable day, and that -- save the one exception -- is not ours to give you.

We cannot tell you what excavation would turn up, if a trench were opened where we gathered. No site report or catalogue of inscriptions has been read to answer that. What we can give you is what one pastoral letter describes. There was an apse, a raised seating area for the clergy, steps leading up to it, and a floor for the congregation. That evidence comes from the letter, not from a dig. It tells us something real about the setting of our worship, but it is not a plan of the building or an account of what stone and mortar would survive.

We also have no inscription of our own that marks our worship as distinct, the way the rival communion has one. Material evidence for this region exists, but it has not yet been read for what it shows of how we gathered. So what the ground itself would give back to someone digging now, we cannot say.

We asked a great deal, and we lost people over it. During the persecution, Rome demanded a sacrifice. The demand reached each person alone. Some stood and would not do it. Others complied -- some by sacrificing, some only by paying for a paper saying they had. Both ways counted as giving in, and both left a person outside the table until a road back was walked.

What we asked, first, was that a person refuse compliance when the order came. That refusal could cost you your freedom, your body, or your life. The confessors were the ones who held firm when questioned and lived. Their suffering was real, and so was what it carried. Some who gave way asked to come back, and we brought them back -- but not the moment they asked, and not without a road walked in the open where the same people who watched them fall were the ones who had to receive them.

We also asked that a person, once baptized, live differently. Cyprian wrote a whole treatise to the rich among us, telling them plainly what their wealth was for: share your gains with Christ. Augustine taught that almsgiving is the ordinary remedy for sin after baptism, since baptism washes sin away once. A rich believer who withheld it was refusing the cure God had given.

And we asked, at the point of coming in, that a person be taught what they were joining before they joined it. You learned the creed, you said it back, and then you were baptized. That teaching took time. It was not a transaction completed in a moment.

The cost of belonging was greatest for those who stood when the order came. Cyprian himself was beheaded on 14 September 258. The confessors in prison with him had already borne interrogation, chains, and hunger. That is what we asked, and that is what some gave.

Augustine defended marriage as a real good, against those who thought praising virginity meant condemning it. He named three things it is good for: offspring, faithfulness between the two, and what he called its sacrament. Of that third good he wrote this: a marriage compact is entered into as a matter of a certain sacrament, and it is not made void even by separation. So long as her husband lives, a wife who marries another while separated from him still commits adultery. This is not a rule about how to behave at someone else's wedding. It is a teaching about what marriage itself is, and what it binds.

Beyond that teaching, we cannot tell you much. We have nothing that describes the wedding itself — no account of how a couple came together, what words were said over them, or how the congregation marked it. Augustine wrote to defend what marriage is, not to describe how it was done. What we can say is that he held it as a binding covenant, not dissolved by separation, and that it served three clear ends: children, faithfulness, and a sacramental bond. The rest — courtship, ceremony, the rite itself — is simply not where our record was formed.

Yes. The teaching on unbaptized infants unsettled us, and we did not hide that it was hard.

We baptized infants, and we would not make a newborn wait. Cyprian and his colleagues met in council, sixty-six in number, and wrote to Fidus. He had thought a child should not be baptized before the eighth day. "No one agreed," they wrote.

Augustine went on to the hard end of this. In his book On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins he named the unbaptized.

Neither bishop tells us of any one child. We hold the teaching as it stands, and we do not pretend it sits lightly.
